title: Mitridate, re di Ponto, K. 87: Overture
description: Mozart was 14 when his first opera seria, “Mithridates, King of Pontus,” opened on 26 December 1770 at the Teatro Regio Ducale, the court theatre in the Palazzo Reale palace beside the Duomo. That theatre burned in 1776; La Scala replaced it.

title: L’elisir d’amore: Una furtiva lagrima
description: Donizetti’s comic opera “The Elixir of Love” premiered in 1832 at the Teatro della Canobbiana, now the Teatro Lirico on Via Larga. This tenor aria, “A furtive tear,” is its best-known number. The theatre was renamed for singer Giorgio Gaber in 2021.

title: Nabucco: Va, pensiero
place: Casa Verdi rest home, Piazza Buonarroti
description: The Hebrew slaves’ chorus, “Go, thought, on golden wings,” made Verdi’s name at La Scala in 1842. When his body was moved in 1901 to the rest home for musicians he founded, Casa Verdi on Piazza Buonarroti, crowds sang it. He lies in its crypt.

title: Messa da Requiem: Dies irae
description: Verdi wrote his Requiem to honour novelist Alessandro Manzoni, author of “The Betrothed,” and conducted the first performance on 22 May 1874 in San Marco church in Brera, a year after Manzoni’s death. “Dies irae” means “day of wrath.”

title: Madama Butterfly: Un bel dì vedremo
description: Puccini’s “Madama Butterfly” was booed at its La Scala premiere on 17 February 1904. He withdrew it, revised it, and it triumphed in Brescia months later. In Cio-Cio-San’s aria, “One fine day we’ll see,” she hopes that her American husband returns.

title: O mia bela Madunina
description: Songwriter Giovanni D’Anzi’s dialect anthem, “Oh my beautiful little Madonna,” salutes the gilded Virgin on the highest spire of the Duomo cathedral, a Milanese symbol since 1774. Fans still sing it at the San Siro stadium.

title: Ma mi
description: Theatre director Giorgio Strehler wrote these dialect words, “But me,” for singer Ornella Vanoni (1934–2025): a resistance prisoner held in San Vittore prison who refuses to name names. It belongs to her “canzoni della mala,” songs of the Milan underworld.

title: Porta Romana
description: Milanese singer and theatre-maker Giorgio Gaber (1939–2003) sings of the working-class streets and bars around Porta Romana, the 1596 stone gate on the old Spanish walls where the road to Rome left the city.

title: Il ragazzo della via Gluck
description: Adriano Celentano grew up at No. 14 on Via Gluck, behind the Central Station. “The boy from Via Gluck” mourns the fields there lost to postwar concrete, an early Italian protest song about urban sprawl, sung at the 1966 Sanremo festival.

title: Vengo anch’io. No, tu no
place: Derby Club site, Viale Monte Rosa
description: Doctor, songwriter and comic Enzo Jannacci (1935–2013) had his biggest hit with this absurdist refrain, “I’m coming too. No, not you.” He was a pillar of the Derby Club on Viale Monte Rosa, the cabaret where Milan’s satirical comedy scene grew up.

title: Luci a San Siro
description: Songwriter Roberto Vecchioni remembers courting by car in the dark near the San Siro stadium: “Lights at San Siro,” with the floodlights of Inter and AC Milan’s shared ground as the backdrop. It became one of the best-loved Milan songs.

title: Badabum Cha Cha
description: Rapper Marracash, born Fabio Bartolo Rizzo to Sicilian parents, grew up in the Barona housing estates on Milan’s southwest edge. This lead single from his 2008 debut album helped take Milan street rap into the Italian charts.

title: Tran Tran
description: Sfera Ebbasta, real name Gionata Boschetti, comes from Cinisello Balsamo, a commuter town just north of Milan, and built Italian trap there with producer Charlie Charles. The title is slang for the daily grind; the town square is Piazza Gramsci.

title: Cara Italia
description: Ghali Amdouni, son of Tunisian parents, grew up in Baggio on Milan’s western outskirts. “Dear Italy” is a love letter to the country that questions who counts as Italian, from a rapper born and raised in Milan.

title: Soldi
description: Singer Mahmood, Sardinian mother and Egyptian father, grew up in Gratosoglio, the high-rise estate on Milan’s southern edge. “Money” is about a father who left, with an Arabic line; it won Sanremo in 2019 and came second at Eurovision.
